questions.q: What is Sentinel's default pricing model?
options: Pay-as-you-go, billed per gigabyte of data ingested per day into the workspace
A one-time flat fee regardless of data volume
Billed per analyst seat, with no relationship to data volume
Free for any amount of data, with no cost at all
questions.explain: Sentinel is billed pay-as-you-go by default, based on GB of data ingested per day into the Log Analytics workspace.

questions.q: Why would an organization choose a commitment tier over pay-as-you-go pricing?
options: Its daily ingestion volume is large and fairly consistent, so a fixed-volume discounted rate costs less than pure pay-as-you-go
Commitment tiers are required before any connector can be enabled
Pay-as-you-go pricing does not exist for Sentinel
Commitment tiers are only available for workspaces with zero data
questions.explain: Commitment tiers trade flexibility for a discounted per-GB rate once an organization's ingestion is steady and high-volume.

options: The free window during which ingested data stays normally queryable before additional storage cost applies
A feature that lets analysts chat with Sentinel using natural language
The maximum number of analysts who can be logged in at once
A setting that deletes all data immediately after ingestion
questions.explain: Interactive retention is the included, free period where data remains queryable; keeping it longer costs extra per GB per month.

questions.q: Why isn't the archive tier suitable for day-to-day detection work?
options: Archived data isn't instantly queryable — accessing it requires a search job or restore operation first, which takes time
Archive tier data is automatically deleted after 24 hours
Archive tier only stores data from third-party firewalls
Archive tier costs more per GB than interactive retention
questions.explain: Archive is cheap long-term storage, but getting data back out requires a search job or restore, unlike normally queryable interactive retention.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what real decision does a Sentinel administrator have to make for each data source?
options: Whether it's valuable enough for active detection to justify its ingestion/retention cost, or whether archive is the cheaper fit once it ages out of active use
Whether to disable all data connectors to avoid any cost whatsoever
Whether KQL or SQL should be used to query it, which is purely a personal preference
Whether to store it exclusively on local hardware instead of in the workspace
questions.explain: Balancing active-detection value against ingestion/retention cost, with archive as the cheaper long-term option, is a real recurring cost decision.
